analysis.one_liner: Blocked the Labor Department from stripping overtime pay from workers currently eligible.
analysis.headline: Despite 55 cosponsors — 47 Democrats and 8 Republicans, led by a Republican — the bill never received a House vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to stop the Secretary of Labor from writing any new rule that moves workers out of overtime eligibility, freezing the list of exempt jobs as it stood when the bill passed. It explicitly allowed the Secretary to expand overtime to cover more workers, but not to shrink it. The bill went to the House Education and Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended — no markup, no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers whose jobs could have been reclassified as exempt — that is, workers who could have lost the right to time-and-a-half pay for hours over 40 — keep their overtime protection. Any worker the Labor Department later moved into overtime eligibility would gain as well.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at risk of losing overtime

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred the Secretary of Labor from promulgating any regulation that has the effect of exempting from overtime requirements any employee not already exempt under rules in effect at enactment.
It explicitly preserved the Secretary's power to reduce the number of exempt employees — that is, to extend overtime protection to more workers, but never to fewer.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of salaried white-collar workers, who would face higher payroll costs whenever the Labor Department expanded overtime coverage, and who would lose the ability to have new rules move whole groups of employees out of overtime eligibility.

drawbacks.text: Employers would bear higher labor costs whenever the Secretary moved more workers into overtime eligibility, a cost some would pass on through reduced hours or hiring.

Freezing the exemption list as of enactment would prevent the Department from updating overtime rules to reflect changes in job duties and pay levels over time, a flexibility an honest supporter would have to give up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and directly tied to take-home pay for millions of workers who could have been reclassified out of overtime. The costs are higher employer payroll costs and a rigid, frozen exemption list that cannot adapt to new job categories. The bill is blunt — a statutory freeze rather than a recalibrated rule — but its main effect is to keep a guaranteed pay right where it stood.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Education and Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it sat with no markup or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 8, 2003 by Rep. Peter King of New York, joined by seven original cosponsors from both parties, and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on July 21, 2003, and no further action was ever recorded on it.
The bill gathered 55 cosponsors — 47 Democrats and 8 Republicans — but never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of salaried office workers came out ahead: the bill would have barred the Labor Department from writing rules that reclassify employees out of overtime eligibility, and with the bill dead, the Department's rulemaking could proceed unimpeded.

for.name: Rep. Peter T. King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. George Miller of California
for.role: Original cosponsor, senior Democrat on the Education and Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: 8 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside the Republican sponsor.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and then a subcommittee and was never scheduled for a markup or floor vote; it died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: The Bush administration
against.role: White House and Department of Labor
against.what_they_did: The Labor Department was rewriting the overtime rules that this bill was designed to block, and the administration opposed congressional efforts to stop the new rules from taking effect.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill and 55 members cosigned it — 47 Democrats and 8 Republicans — yet the Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Employers of salaried white-collar workers (retail, restaurants, insurance, financial services)
industries.note: The bill would have barred the Labor Department from writing rules that exempt more employees from overtime, leaving these employers exposed to paying time-and-a-half to workers they could otherwise reclassify. Their interest in killing it ran directly against the pay of the affected workers.
These workers keep their legal right to overtime pay under the bill's freeze on new exemptions; their gain is employers' cost, dollar for dollar.
